### Problem: Minimum number of removals to make a mountain array {#sec-lis-p3-mount}

::: {.p-statement}
A mountain array climbs strictly and then falls strictly, with at least one element on each side of the peak. Return the minimum number of removals that leave a mountain subsequence. The relative order stays.

$3 \le n \le 1000$. On $[1, 3, 1]$ the answer is 0. On $[2, 1, 1, 5, 6, 2, 3, 1]$ the answer is 3: one longest mountain is $2, 5, 6, 2, 1$.

Source: [LC 1671 · Minimum Number of Removals to Make Mountain Array](https://leetcode.com/problems/minimum-number-of-removals-to-make-mountain-array/){.solved difficulty="Hard"}
:::

::: {.p-intuition}
Fewest removals means the longest thing you keep. What you keep is a mountain subsequence: some peak index, a strict increase into it, and a strict decrease out of it. The left arm is an LIS ending at the peak. The right arm is an LIS ending at the peak in the reversed array. Both arms must have length at least 2, otherwise the peak has an empty side.
:::

::: {.p-approach}
- **Left.** $left[i]$ = LIS length ending at $i$.
- **Right.** $right[i]$ = longest strict decrease starting at $i$, computed as an LIS on the reversed array.
- **Peak.** If both are at least 2, the mountain length is $left[i] + right[i] - 1$.
- **Answer.** $n - \max$ of those lengths. The peak is counted in both arms, so it is subtracted once.
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Why the tallest value can be the wrong peak"}
In $[1, 10, 2, 3, 4, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1]$ the value 10 has a left arm of length 2 and a long right arm, keeping 7 and removing 3. The peak 5 keeps $1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1$, nine elements, one removal. The formula tries every index. A strict slope uses the first tail that is $\ge$ the new value. A non-decreasing slope would treat $[5, 5, 5, 1, 6, 5]$ as a slope and report the wrong number of removals.
:::

::: {#fig-lis-peak}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    a = [1, 10, 2, 3, 4, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1]
    n = len(a)
    left, right = [1] * n, [1] * n
    for i in range(n):
        for j in range(i):
            if a[j] < a[i]:
                left[i] = max(left[i], left[j] + 1)
    for i in range(n - 1, -1, -1):
        for k in range(i + 1, n):
            if a[i] > a[k]:
                right[i] = max(right[i], right[k] + 1)
    best, peak = 0, 0
    for i in range(n):
        if left[i] >= 2 and right[i] >= 2 and left[i] + right[i] - 1 > best:
            best, peak = left[i] + right[i] - 1, i
    assert best == 9 and a[peak] == 5 and left[1] + right[1] - 1 == 7
    colors = {i: ("amber" if i == 1 else "green") for i in range(n)}
    V.bars(ax, p, a, colors=colors, height=3.4)
V.show(draw)
```

Green is the mountain of length 9 whose peak is 5. Amber is the 10: using it as the peak keeps only 7.

:::

The buttons are in order. Each one keeps the previous solution and changes only what that form changes.

::: {.panel-tabset .solution-forms}

#### Recursion

::: {.form-next}
`f(i)` is the rising length ending at `i`, the same recursion as an LIS. The falling length is that recursion on the reversed array. A peak needs both lengths at least 2. The removals are `n` minus the longest such mountain.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("mount", "rec")
    assert str(final) == "3"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
#| label: mount-rec
def mount_rec(a):
    def arm(b):
        def f(i):
            best = 1
            for j in range(i):
                if b[j] < b[i]:
                    best = max(best, 1 + f(j))
            return best
        return [f(i) for i in range(len(b))]

    left, right = arm(a), arm(a[::-1])[::-1]
    keep = 0
    for i in range(len(a)):
        if left[i] >= 2 and right[i] >= 2:
            keep = max(keep, left[i] + right[i] - 1)
    return len(a) - keep
```

##### C++

```cpp
int mountArm(int i, const vector<int>& b) {
    int best = 1;
    for (int j = 0; j < i; ++j)
        if (b[j] < b[i]) best = max(best, 1 + mountArm(j, b));
    return best;
}
```
:::

#### Memo

::: {.form-next}
Each arm has `n` endings. Store them. The peak scan is the same line as the recursion's last loop.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("mount", "memo")
    assert str(final) == "3"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
#| label: mount-memo
def mount_memo(a):
    def arm(b):
        memo = [-1] * len(b)

        def f(i):
            if memo[i] < 0:
                best = 1
                for j in range(i):
                    if b[j] < b[i]:
                        best = max(best, 1 + f(j))
                memo[i] = best
            return memo[i]

        return [f(i) for i in range(len(b))]

    left, right = arm(a), arm(a[::-1])[::-1]
    keep = 0
    for i in range(len(a)):
        if left[i] >= 2 and right[i] >= 2:
            keep = max(keep, left[i] + right[i] - 1)
    return len(a) - keep
```

##### C++

```cpp
int mountMemo(int i, const vector<int>& b, vector<int>& memo) {
    if (memo[i] >= 0) return memo[i];
    int best = 1;
    for (int j = 0; j < i; ++j)
        if (b[j] < b[i]) best = max(best, 1 + mountMemo(j, b, memo));
    return memo[i] = best;
}
```
:::

#### Two tables

::: {.form-next}
Replace each arm by the $O(n^2)$ LIS table. `left` is filled on `a`. `right` is the same table on the reversed array, written back into the original index order. Subtract one for the shared peak.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("mount", "tab")
    assert str(final) == "3"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
#| label: mount-tab
def _lis_row(a):
    end = [1] * len(a)
    for i in range(len(a)):
        for j in range(i):
            if a[j] < a[i]:
                end[i] = max(end[i], end[j] + 1)
    return end

def mount_tab(a):
    left, right = _lis_row(a), _lis_row(a[::-1])[::-1]
    keep = 0
    for i in range(len(a)):
        if left[i] >= 2 and right[i] >= 2:
            keep = max(keep, left[i] + right[i] - 1)
    return len(a) - keep
```

##### C++

```cpp
vector<int> lisRow(const vector<int>& a) {
    int n = a.size();
    vector<int> end(n, 1);
    for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i)
        for (int j = 0; j < i; ++j)
            if (a[j] < a[i]) end[i] = max(end[i], end[j] + 1);
    return end;
}
```
:::

#### Tails

::: {.form-next}
The length ending at each index is the slot the tails array assigns, plus one. Run that scan forward for the rising arm and on the reversed array for the falling arm. $n = 1000$ allows the table; the tails form is the same algorithm at $10^5$.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("mount", "tails")
    assert str(final) == "3"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
#| label: mount-tails
def _lis_at(a):
    tails, at = [], []
    for x in a:
        lo, hi = 0, len(tails)
        while lo < hi:
            mid = (lo + hi) // 2
            if tails[mid] >= x:
                hi = mid
            else:
                lo = mid + 1
        if lo == len(tails):
            tails.append(x)
        else:
            tails[lo] = x
        at.append(lo + 1)
    return at

def mount_tails(a):
    left, right = _lis_at(a), _lis_at(a[::-1])[::-1]
    keep = 0
    for i in range(len(a)):
        if left[i] >= 2 and right[i] >= 2:
            keep = max(keep, left[i] + right[i] - 1)
    return len(a) - keep

long = [2, 1, 1, 5, 6, 2, 3, 1]
assert mount_rec([1, 3, 1]) == mount_memo([1, 3, 1]) == mount_tab([1, 3, 1]) == 0
assert mount_rec(long) == mount_memo(long) == mount_tab(long) == mount_tails(long) == 3
hill = [1, 10, 2, 3, 4, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1]
assert mount_tab(hill) == mount_tails(hill) == 1
```

##### C++

```cpp
int mountTails(const vector<int>& a) {
    auto at = [](const vector<int>& b) {
        vector<int> tails, len;
        for (int x : b) {
            int lo = 0, hi = tails.size();
            while (lo < hi) {
                int mid = (lo + hi) / 2;
                if (tails[mid] >= x) hi = mid;
                else lo = mid + 1;
            }
            if (lo == (int)tails.size()) tails.push_back(x);
            else tails[lo] = x;
            len.push_back(lo + 1);
        }
        return len;
    };
    vector<int> rev(a.rbegin(), a.rend());
    auto left = at(a), rr = at(rev);
    int n = a.size(), keep = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) {
        int right = rr[n - 1 - i];
        if (left[i] >= 2 && right >= 2) keep = max(keep, left[i] + right - 1);
    }
    return n - keep;
}
```
:::

:::

::: {.p-complexity}
The recursive arms are for the two short samples. **Memoisation** and the **two tables** are $O(n^2)$. **Tails** is $O(n \log n)$. $n \le 1000$ allows the tables. The answer is a count of removals, so it is $n - K$ and not $K$.
:::

::: {.p-edge}
- $[1, 3, 1]$ is already a mountain: 0 removals.
- Both arms must be non-empty. An index at an end of the array has an arm of length 1 and is not a peak.
- If no index has two real arms, the subtraction uses a kept length of 0 and returns $n$.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistakes"}
- Counting the peak twice. $left + right$ includes $i$ in both. The length is $left + right - 1$. On the long sample that is 5, and the removals are 3, not 2.
- Accepting an arm of length 1. A single element is not a slope. $[1, 2, 3]$ has no mountain.
- A non-decreasing arm. Equals are not a strict climb. `upper_bound` is the wrong binary search here.
:::

**Variants.** The minimum sum of an index triple $i < j < k$ with $a[i] < a[j]$ and $a[k] < a[j]$ is the same peak, asked for three positions only: [LC 2909 · Minimum Sum of Mountain Triplets II](https://leetcode.com/problems/minimum-sum-of-mountain-triplets-ii/){difficulty="Medium"}. A mountain subarray, which cannot skip, is a run of rising steps followed by falling steps: [LC 845 · Longest Mountain in Array](https://leetcode.com/problems/longest-mountain-in-array/){difficulty="Medium"}. Up and down as two rolling lengths is the wiggle subsequence: [LC 376 · Wiggle Subsequence](https://leetcode.com/problems/wiggle-subsequence/){difficulty="Medium"}. Which indices sit on some LIS, or on every LIS, is the forward length plus the backward length: [CF 486E · LIS of Sequence](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/486/E){rating="2200"}.
